thread.title: The Apple Watch will be tested in a joint surgery study (AAPL)

author: Nicky Lineaweaver
title: The Apple Watch will be tested in a joint surgery study (AAPL)

organizations.name: business insider intelligence " digital health brie

text:
This story was delivered to Business Insider Intelligence " Digital Health Briefing " subscribers hours before appearing on Business Insider. To be the first to know, please click here .
Apple is partnering with medical device company Zimmer Biomet to test how the Apple Watch can improve health outcomes and reduce costs for knee and hip replacement surgeries. This latest thrust in Apple's evolving healthcare push aims to eventually enroll 10,000 patients in what the companies call "one of the largest evidence-gathering clinical studies in orthopedic history."
Business Insider Intelligence
The study will incorporate the new Zimmer Biomet mymobility app, which facilitates communication between a patient and their care team. Providers can view continuous Apple Watch data on a patient's heart rate, step count, and time spent standing to inform feedback that helps the patient prepare for operation and streamlines recovery.
Payers and healthcare providers can benefit from the joint study. As an example, a care team that sees a patient is over-exerting themselves after an operation could send the patient a reminder to limit the number of steps they take, which may reduce the likelihood of complications and unnecessary hospitalizations. That could reduce insurers' risk of paying out for additional treatment.
And providers could benefit as the partnership improves the patient experience by increasing engagement between patients and care providers, in turn maximizing reimbursement under value-based care (VBC). VBC is a reimbursement model in which providers are paid based on positive patient outcomes rather than the number of services the patient.
The new Apple Watch study is the latest indicator that the tech giant is eyeing baby boomers as the crux of its healthcare play. The Apple Watch 4 — which was released in September — received FDA clearance for an electrocardiogram app and its ability to detect atrial fibrillation. Both of these features address conditions that disproportionately affect older consumers.
Similarly, the number of knee and hip replacement surgeries is expected to triple to 3.5 million by 2035 alongside a boom in the senior population — 22% of Americans ( 81 million people) will be 65 years or older by 2040, up from 15% in 2016.
Business Insider Intelligence's exclusive data provides strong evidence that suggests Apple's bet on the senior healthcare market will pay off.In an informal survey of 1,709 Business Insider readers, Business Insider Intelligence found that 48% of baby boomers say they're going to buy the new Apple Watch — exceeding the share of Gen Xers (46%), millennials (35%), and Gen Zers (29%) who said the same.
While the survey data isn't representative of the general population — Business Insider readers tend to be younger, male, and tech-savvy — the results provide strong evidence that Apple's push for the senior healthcare market via the Apple Watch Series 4 has some legs.
